about: Round 21b hidden-secret battery (tester, phase A). Offline: every case is a context text, the hidden line numbers the brief's rule gives, the exact text for the prompt and the values that must not appear anywhere in the driver's output. All values are made up and only match the SHAPE rules of EzraSecretDetector.textHoldsCredentialShape. Expected numbers come from lib_oracle.mjs, an independent implementation, and equal the author's intent for every case (the generator fails otherwise).
how_to_use: check_driver_records.mjs --cases this file --records <driver prepare output of the same ids> checks, per case: contextHiddenLineCount; the user text after the heading in contextBlockText equals expect.textForPrompt (null block when contextBlockPresent is false); contextCharacterCount; systemBlocks has 3 blocks with a block and 2 without; and no hiddenValue or hiddenValueFragment occurs in any string of the record (systemBlocks, systemPromptText, static and dynamic text, contextBlockText).
ambiguities: A1: after 'their words:' the brief does not say whether one newline or a blank line follows. extractUserTextFromBlock accepts either (it removes the heading through 'their words:' and then up to two leading newlines).

A2: 'trimmed of leading and trailing blank lines' is read as: whitespace-only lines at the start and end are dropped; the first and last kept line keep their own leading and trailing spaces. Cases avoid indentation on the first and last kept line so a stricter trim (whitespacesAndNewlines) gives the same result.
A3: the cut to 2,000 characters is a plain prefix of the joined text; nothing is trimmed again after the cut. Cases that are cut end on a non-space character so both readings agree.

A4: contextHiddenLineCount counts hidden lines over the FULL text, including hidden lines that lie beyond the 2,000 character cut (the brief: numbers are computed on the full text as the editor shows it).

A5: String.count is the number of extended grapheme clusters; the oracle uses Intl.Segmenter (granularity grapheme). Unicode-version differences between ICU/Swift and Node could differ for exotic emoji; the emoji case uses a flag, a ZWJ sequence and a combining mark, which agree.

my notes app is bear, and i keep one note per project, named after the project's folder on disk.
on mondays i plan the week, on fridays i write a short review of what shipped and what slipped.
i prefer small pull requests, one idea each, with a title that says what changed and why it matters.
my keyboard is a split one, so shortcuts that need two hands on the left side are painful for me.
when something breaks i want the likely cause first, then the fix, then how to check that it worked.
i review designs on a second monitor, so questions about the left screen usually mean the primary one.
my team is three people: one backend, one mobile, and me, and we meet every day at nine fifteen sharp.
i read documentation in the browser and take notes in the editor, so keep that split in mind please.
the staging environment resets every night, so anything i test there is gone by the next morning.
i like examples more than rules: one small example beats a paragraph of explanation for me every time.
i commute by train, so i often ask short questions on my phone and expect short answers back as well.
i write swift for the app, typescript for the worker, and a little shell for glue between the two parts.
my editor font is large because i work with the screen further away than most people usually do at all.
i keep a changelog by hand, one line per change, newest first, and i never rewrite lines already there.
when i say the proxy i mean the worker in front of the model api, not the corporate network proxy at all.
i back up on sundays and test a restore once a month, which i learned the hard way a few years ago now.
my calendar blocks the mornings for deep work, so i prefer to hear about meetings in the afternoon only.
i name branches with a short prefix and a ticket number, for example fix and then the number, then a word.
the office wifi is flaky on the third floor, so a failed request there is usually the network, not the code.
i test on the oldest supported macos first, because that is where most of the surprises have come from so far.
i keep the release checklist in a text file next to the project and tick the boxes off one by one as i go.
if a question is about a color i usually mean the design token, not the raw hex value used inside the file.
i like to hear which file a change belongs in before hearing the change itself, since i jump between files a lot.
